Some EDA

Overlook of all industries

The first part lists all the industries from the data, as I want to overlook all the industries in the daily_visit data set to better understand how I can create the visualization and tell the story. Since food is one of the most crucial things in our lives and there are many great restaurants and food markets in the area, I want to explore people’s eating habits in the King County area.

all1<-dv%>%
  select(naics_title,date)%>%
  drop_na()

all1<-all1%>%
  distinct(naics_title)

Restaurant:Comparion of Full-Service restaurants and Limited-Service restaurants

To start with, I want to get a big picture of the customer’s visits to the dine-in restaurants. The restaurants are categorized into Full-Service and Limited-Service based on the service. Full-Service Restaurants are defined as a restaurant where meals are primarily prepared individually for the customer and are served to customers at their table by wait staff. A Limited-Service restaurant is a restaurant in which service is kept to a minimum, and a customer’s interactions with staff and when the customer receives their food, such as a fast-food restaurant or restaurant with has drive-through facilities. Comparing the customer’s visits to two types of restaurant allows us to see which dine-in experience locals are more gravitate towards.

limited <- dv %>% 
  filter(naics_title == "Limited-Service Restaurants") %>% 
  group_by(brands) %>%
  summarise(Total_Visits = sum(visits_by_day)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(Total_Visits))
full <- dv %>% 
  filter(naics_title == "Full-Service Restaurants") %>% 
  group_by(brands) %>%
  summarise(Total_Visits = sum(visits_by_day)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(Total_Visits))
limited_visits <- limited %>%
  summarise(Limited_service = sum(Total_Visits))%>%
  mutate(Resturant_type='Limited_Service')%>%
  rename( 'Visits' = Limited_service)
full_visits <- full%>%
  summarise(Full_service = sum(Total_Visits))%>%
  mutate(Resturant_type='Full_Service')%>%
  rename( 'Visits' = Full_service)

full_and_limited<-rbind(full_visits,limited_visits)

show(full_and_limited)
## # A tibble: 2 × 2
##   Visits Resturant_type 
##    <int> <chr>          
## 1 349655 Full_Service   
## 2 232464 Limited_Service

Comparion of Full-Service resturant and Limited-Service resturants in Graph

all_restaurant_comparion<-full_and_limited%>%
  ggplot(aes(x=Resturant_type, y=Visits, fill=Resturant_type))+geom_col()+scale_fill_brewer(palette = 'Paired')+
  labs(title = 'Customers Visits of Full-Service and Limited-Service Resturant', subtitle = "In July 2020, ZKing County")+
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5), plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) + 
  xlab('Resturant Type') + 
  ylab('Customer Visits')+
  theme(legend.position = "none", 
      panel.grid.major = element_blank(), 
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma)+
  geom_text(aes(label=Visits,
                y=Visits),
            vjust=2)

all_restaurant_comparion

The graph shows that full-service restaurants in King County have more customer visits than the limited-service restaurants in July 2022. With more than 33% of customer visits, we can conclude that locals gravitate more towards full-service restaurants when dining out.

What are the top 10 full-service restaurants and their total visit in July 2020 in King County?

After knowing full-service restaurants have more customer visits than limited-service restaurants, I want to see which full-service restaurants have the most visits in the area. As the data set contains some empty cells in the brand column, I think it’s better to keep only the restaurants with the brand names on the top 10 list for better analysis.

#select all the full service restaurants
full_service_restaurants <- dv %>% 
  filter(naics_title == "Full-Service Restaurants") %>% 
  group_by(brands) %>%
  summarise(Total_Visits = sum(visits_by_day)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(Total_Visits))

#delete the blank row
full_service_restaurants <- full_service_restaurants %>%
  filter(Total_Visits <= 10000)

#select top 10 restaurants
top10restaurants <- full_service_restaurants %>%
  head(10)
show(top10restaurants)

The graph shows that MOD Pizza has the most visits among all the top 10 full-service restaurants, which double customer visits of second on the list (Ivar’s SeaFood). The Rest all-service restaurants have about 3000-1500 customer visits in July 2020. We can also get an idea that Pizza is probably the first option for many locals when eating out. To get a more insightful analysis of the locals’ restaurant choices, I suggest getting the data on their number of locations and where they are located. By cross-comparing the total visits and the number of locations, we can see the factors that affect customers’ visits to the full-service restaurant.

Top 5 Full Service Restaurant’s Customer Living Locations

Next, I want to see the living locations with the most average customers visit for the full-service restaurants in July 2020. This allows us to see the living district distribution of the full-service restaurant’s customers. By looking at the data and graph, we can know people who live in certain areas have a higher tendency to eat out at the full-service restaurant. Restaurants can use this data to determine where to open the new locations will gain more customer visits.

Full_neighborhood_names <- ov %>% 
  right_join(neighborhood_names) %>% 
  filter(naics_title == "Full-Service Restaurants")
## Joining, by = "GEOID"
Full_Living_Area_Top5 <- Full_neighborhood_names %>% 
  group_by(NEIGHBORHOOD_DISTRICT_NAME) %>% 
  summarise(Avg_Customer_visits = round(mean(visits), digits = 2)) %>%
  arrange(-Avg_Customer_visits) %>% 
  slice(1:5)

Full_Living_Area_Top5
## # A tibble: 5 × 2
##   NEIGHBORHOOD_DISTRICT_NAME Avg_Customer_visits

## 2 East                                      36.7
## 3 Lake Union                                36.5
## 4 Central                                   33.5
## 5 Ballard                                   33.4

Top 5 Full-Service Restaurant’s Customer Living Location with the Average Visits

Full_Living_Area_Top5_Graph <- Full_Living_Area_Top5%>%
  ggplot(aes(x=reorder(NEIGHBORHOOD_DISTRICT_NAME,Avg_Customer_visits),y=Avg_Customer_visits, fill = NEIGHBORHOOD_DISTRICT_NAME))+ geom_col()+
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Downtown" = "#AA0000",
                                "East" = "#C0422A",
                                "Lake Union" = "#D36A51",
                                "Central" = "#E38F6A",
                                "Ballard" = "#F0B4A4"
                               )) +
  labs(title = "Top 5 Full-Service Restaurant's Customer Original Location", 
       subtitle = "By Average Visits in July 2020")+
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5), 
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) +
  xlab("Living Areas") + 
  ylab("Average Visits") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Avg_Customer_visits, 
              y = Avg_Customer_visits), 
          vjust = -0.5)+
  theme(legend.position = "none", 
      panel.grid.major = element_blank(), 
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank())+
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,45), expand = c(0,0))

Full_Living_Area_Top5_Graph

I use bar chart to list and compare the top 5 locations with the most average full-service restaurant customer visits, for it give a clear overview of the list. The graph shows that residents live in visit full-service restaurant the most in July 202, and all the top 5 areas are all in Seattle. Full-service restaurant can use this analysis insight to choose their new locations and determine their target customers and advertisement plan for each location.

Food Markets:Overview Trend of Food Markets and Stores:

Meat Markets,Fish and Seafood Markets, Fruit and Vegetable Markets, and Baked Goods Stores.

After exploring the restaurant industry in the previous part, in the next part of the analysis, I will be exploring the overview of customer visits to the food markets and stores in the area. I choose 4 different categories: Meat Markets, Fish and Seafood Markets, Fruit and Vegetable Markets, and Baked Goods Stores to see the grocery shopping trend.

I want to take a look of the daily customer visits of food markets throughout the month of July in 2020 to see the grocery shopping trend, and compare the customer visits of each category.

all2<-filter(dv, naics_title %in% c('Meat Markets','Fish and Seafood Markets','Fruit and Vegetable Markets','Baked Goods Stores'))%>%
  select(date, naics_title,visits_by_day)%>%
  rename(Food_Category=naics_title)

Showing food market and store customer visit of July 2020

allfoodgp<-
  ggplot(all2, aes(x = date, y = visits_by_day, colour = Food_Category)) +geom_line()+
  xlab("Date") + ylab("Daily Visits")+
  labs(title = "Customer Visits Trend of Food Market and Stores ", subtitle = "In July 2020")+
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5), plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))+
    theme(legend.position = "right", 
          legend.key.height= unit(0.3, 'cm'),
           legend.key.width= unit(0.3, 'cm'),
        panel.grid.major = element_blank(), 
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) 

allfoodgp

The line graph shows the trend of the industry throughout the month of July. All the categories seem to always fall on certain dates together. This suggests that customers tend to go to markets on certain days, and purchase all the needed items at once. The graph also shows fruit and vegetable category and fish and seafood category have the most customer visits, and baked goods stores have the less customer visits. I suggest to also look at consumption data of each category to get the better insights of the market demand.

Top 5 Food Market and Store’s Customer Living Locations

Food_Category_location <- ov %>% 
  right_join(neighborhood_names) %>% 
  filter(naics_title %in% c('Meat Markets','Fish and Seafood Markets','Fruit and Vegetable Markets','Baked Goods Stores'))
## Joining, by = "GEOID"
Food_Category_location_ <- Food_Category_location %>% 
  group_by(NEIGHBORHOOD_DISTRICT_NAME) %>% 
  summarise(Avg_Customer_visits = round(mean(visits), digits = 2)) %>%
  arrange(-Avg_Customer_visits) %>% 
  slice(1:5)

Top 5 Food Market and Store’s Customer Living Locations with Totals Visits in July 2020

The next part, I will be looking for the top locations that have people who and visit food markets and stores. In other word, I want to see residents from in which areas go to grocery shopping more, which can show people live in those areas tend to prepare meal at home more than dinning out.

Food_Category_location_graph <- Food_Category_location_%>%
  ggplot(aes(x=reorder(NEIGHBORHOOD_DISTRICT_NAME,Avg_Customer_visits),y=Avg_Customer_visits, fill = NEIGHBORHOOD_DISTRICT_NAME))+ geom_col()+
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Greater Duwamish" = "#4A4377",
                                "Northeast" = "#6259A2",
                                "Central" = "#7B70D0",
                                "North" = "#AA9BFF",
                                "Delridge Neighborhoods" = "#CEC2FF"
                               )) +
  labs(title = "Top 5 Food Market and Store's Customer Living Location", 
       subtitle = "By Average Visits in July 2020")+
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5), 
        plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) +
  xlab("Living Areas") + 
  ylab("Average Visits") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Avg_Customer_visits, 
              y = Avg_Customer_visits), 
          vjust = -0.5)+
  theme(legend.position = "none", 
      panel.grid.major = element_blank(), 
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank())+
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,8), expand = c(0,0))

Food_Category_location_graph

The graph shows the top 5 food market customer living locations. I can conclude that customers from the south (Greater Duwamish and Delridge Neighborhood), and north areas (North and Northeast) visit food markets most more compare to downtown areas. I suggest getting the data of food markets and stores or the number of restaurants in each district to see the relationship between the customer visits time and number of the market in the Neighborhood.

After exploring the restaurants and food industries of King Country in July 2020, I can conclude that people who live near downtown areas tend to dine in the restaurant more than people who live far away from the city. Also, MOD pizza is a popular restaurant in King County, and the vegetable and seafood market has the most customer visits than meat and bakery stores.
